question:
Patient note:
An 85-year-old widowed man, a retired railroad signal technician who lives alone in a ground-floor apartment and still drives himself to the grocery store, was referred to the comprehensive cardiometabolic clinic this afternoon because of a three-month history of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness that has progressed from climbing a full flight of stairs to becoming winded while carrying two bags of produce from his car; over the past week he has slept propped on two pillows to keep from awakening short of breath and has noticed that his socks leave faint impressions above the ankles by evening. He recalls being told six years ago, after an emergency department visit for influenza complicated by pulmonary edema, that the main pumping chamber of his heart was working at “about one-third of normal.” A follow-up transthoracic echocardiogram performed eight months ago showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 32 % with global hypokinesis, moderate concentric remodeling, mild functional mitral regurgitation, and pulmonary artery systolic pressure estimated at 46 mm Hg; he has taken carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg each morning, and low-dose spironolactone since that time, with only intermittent adherence to sodium restriction. He has never experienced crushing retrosternal pain, diaphoresis during activity, or been rushed to the catheterization laboratory, and serial high-sensitivity troponins obtained during previous admissions for volume overload have remained below the assay limit of detection. Neurologic history is notable only for age-appropriate forgetfulness such as misplacing reading glasses; his daughter, who manages his online bill payments, confirms that he balances his checkbook in pen without difficulty and successfully completed a crossword puzzle yesterday, suggesting preserved orientation, memory, and executive function, and he adamantly denies ever awaking with sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, or facial droop. Pulmonary review is otherwise unremarkable: he never smoked or lived with habitual smokers, has had no chronic cough or episodic bronchospasm, uses no inhalers, and a screening chest radiograph obtained last year for pneumonia follow-up showed clear lung fields with normal diaphragms. Metabolic review reveals that type 2 diabetes was first detected 12 years ago during an annual physical when fasting plasma glucose measured 146 mg/dL on two separate draws; he manages the condition with metformin 1000 mg twice daily and adheres to a balanced plate model recommended by his dietitian. Finger-stick logs brought to clinic demonstrate pre-breakfast values ranging 95–145 mg/dL, and the hemoglobin A1c drawn last week measured 7.2 %. He reports no visual blurring, pedal paresthesias, autonomic symptoms, nephrotic foaming of urine, or foot ulcers, and a dilated retinal examination six months ago documented only mild age-related lens changes without microaneurysms. Hepatic issues surfaced three years ago when mildly elevated aminotransferases (current AST 48 U/L, ALT 52 U/L) were noted during preoperative work-up for a right hemicolectomy; abdominal ultrasound at that time displayed a smooth but slightly echogenic liver measuring 15 cm without splenomegaly, nodularity, or ascites, and viral serologies were negative. Since then he has abstained from alcohol and acetaminophen, maintains albumin 3.9 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1, has never demonstrated peripheral stigmata of portal hypertension, and denies encephalopathic confusion, pruritus, or hematemesis. The hemicolectomy was performed after routine screening colonoscopy revealed a 2.1-cm adenocarcinoma confined to the muscularis propria; surgical margins were clear, 18 regional nodes were negative, postoperative carcinoembryonic antigen normalized, and interval CT imaging at one and two years shows no recurrence or distant disease. Renal indices today include creatinine 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 74 mL/min/1.73 m² and blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL; urinalysis is bland and he produces clear, straw-colored urine without nocturia or flank discomfort. He denies hematemesis, melena, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, or prior ulcer therapy. Current medications also include atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, and a daily multivitamin; he is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which previously provoked diffuse urticaria. Vital signs at 1400 hours show temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 128/66 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 86 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95 % on ambient air; body-mass index is 23 kg/m². He sits comfortably yet speaks in short phrases. Jugular venous pulsation rises to 6 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the apical impulse is laterally displaced to the sixth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line, S1 and S2 are soft, a grade 2/6 holosystolic blowing murmur is heard at the apex radiating toward the axilla, and a third heart sound is audible. Breath sounds are vesicular with faint late-inspiratory crackles at both bases. The abdomen is soft with a smooth liver edge palpable 1 cm below the costal margin, no palpable masses, and normal bowel sounds; the right-sided hemicolectomy scar is well healed without herniation. There is 1+ pitting edema to the mid-shin bilaterally, warm skin, and capillary refill under two seconds; distal pulses are present but slightly diminished by the edema. Neurologic examination reveals a lucid, cooperative gentleman oriented to year, month, and location, with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation, symmetric reflexes, and a narrow-based gait slowed mainly by dyspnea. Laboratory studies drawn on arrival confirm sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white-blood-cell count 6.0 × 10⁹/L, and platelets 212 × 10⁹/L; N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 1840 pg/mL, modestly above his baseline. A 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats/min with left-axis deviation, low voltage in limb leads, and no pathologic Q waves or acute ischemic changes. Chest radiograph demonstrates cardiomegaly, mild pulmonary vascular congestion, and small bilateral pleural effusions. He seeks advice on adjusting diuretics to relieve swelling, whether additional imaging is required to monitor his prior colon malignancy, and strategies to maintain glycemic stability while minimizing salt intake.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index adds age points to weighted comorbidity points, counting only the applicable severity level for each disease:
- Age 85 (≥80 years): 4.
- Congestive heart failure: LVEF 32% with orthopnea, crackles, and edema (1).
- Diabetes without documented end-organ damage: metformin-treated type 2 diabetes without retinopathy, neuropathy, or nephropathy (1).
- Mild chronic liver disease: persistent mild aminotransferase elevation and echogenic liver, with preserved synthetic function and no portal hypertension (1).
- Nonmetastatic solid tumor within five years: localized colon adenocarcinoma resected three years ago (2).
No other Charlson condition is documented. Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
